meta.title: Vishay Precision Group: CEO Ziv Shoshani Steers a Foil-Technology Spinoff Into Humanoid Robotics and AI Infrastructure — Fifteen Years of Precision Measurement Discipline, a Debt-Light Balance Sheet, and an Emerging Design-In Pipeline That Rewrites the Growth Narrative for Bulk Metal Foil Resistors, Strain Gauges, Load Cells, and Industrial Measurement Systems
meta.abstract: Vishay Precision Group (NYSE: VPG) is a Malvern, Pennsylvania-based designer and manufacturer of precision foil resistors, strain gauges, load cells, and industrial measurement systems, spun out of Vishay Intertechnology in July 2010 to pursue an independent strategy focused exclusively on the precision measurement and sensing markets. The company traces its technological lineage to Dr. Felix Zandman, who in the 1950s invented Bulk Metal® Foil technology — a substrate-based resistive process that remains the industry's benchmark for stability, temperature coefficient, and long-term drift performance — and who formally incorporated Vishay Intertechnology in 1962. Under CEO Ziv Shoshani, Dr. Zandman's nephew and a fifteen-year Vishay veteran who assumed the chief executive role at the moment of spinoff, VPG has assembled three distinct reporting segments: Sensors, anchored by foil resistors and Micro-Measurements strain gauges serving defense, avionics, space, and test-and-measurement OEMs; Weighing Solutions, a portfolio of load cells, on-board vehicle weighing systems, and force transducers sold under the BLH Nobel, Stress-Tek, and VPG Transducers brands; and Measurement Systems, which bundles KELK steel-mill gauging platforms, the Gleeble thermal-mechanical simulation franchise (DSI), and laser-based inspection hardware acquired from Germany's Nokra in September 2024. The dossier examines three interlocking strategic narratives: first, how a sub-$350 million revenue business has maintained the technological pedigree and pricing power of a niche monopolist while managing cyclical end-market headwinds; second, how Shoshani's 2025 reorganization — adding a Chief Business and Product Officer and a Chief Operating Officer — positions VPG to capture design-in wins in humanoid robotics, AI infrastructure, and defense electronics at scale; and third, whether the company's debt-light capital structure ($20.6 million long-term debt, $87.4 million cash at year-end 2025), conservative acquisition discipline, and Zandman-family concentrated voting block can sustain a credible multi-year compounding story against larger, better-capitalized metrology rivals. With Q1 2026 bookings crossing $102 million — the first $100 million quarterly booking milestone in company history — the answer the market began pricing in by mid-2026 is cautiously affirmative. Frozen snapshot: 2026-05-23.

chapters.title: The Precision Imperative: VPG at the Inflection
chapters.body:
## A Milestone in the Making

When Vishay Precision Group released its fiscal first-quarter results in May 2026, one number stood apart from the rest. Total bookings for the thirteen weeks ended April 4, 2026 reached $102.1 million — the first time in the company's sixteen-year history as an independent public company that a single quarter had crossed the nine-figure threshold. The book-to-bill ratio of 1.21 implied that demand was arriving faster than VPG could ship it. Management set second-quarter revenue guidance of $85 to $90 million and moved on. But the milestone deserved a longer pause.

That $102.1 million was not the product of a single extraordinary order or a temporary surge in one end market. It reflected demand from defense electronics programs, from AI data-center power-management applications, from industrial weighing and measurement customers resuming deferred capital spending — and, most conspicuously, from at least three humanoid robot developers that had placed prototype orders for the precision force sensors used to give robot joints their sense of proprioception. A Malvern, Pennsylvania company with roughly 2,100 employees, founded on the physics notebooks of a Holocaust survivor turned inventor, had arrived at the center of the most-discussed technology theme in global capital markets.

## Three Pillars, One Dossier

Three interlocking narratives animate the pages that follow.

The first is technological moat. Dr. Felix Zandman — physicist, survivor, and founder — developed the Bulk Metal® Foil resistor in the decades after the Second World War, eventually incorporating Vishay Intertechnology in 1962 and naming the company for the Lithuanian village where his family perished. The foil process he pioneered produces resistors with load-life drift of less than 0.005% and temperature coefficients as low as ±0.2 parts per million per degree Celsius — performance levels that commodity thick-film and thin-film alternatives cannot approach. These specifications are not marketing claims; they are engineering constraints for applications where measurement error is safety-critical: flight-critical avionics, MRI gradient sensing, satellite instrumentation, and now the force-torque loops of robot joints. When Vishay Intertechnology spun off its Precision Group on July 6, 2010, VPG inherited those patents, that manufacturing know-how, and the Micro-Measurements strain gauge heritage — a compound technological endowment that competitors cannot replicate in a product cycle.

The second narrative is timing. Humanoid robotics is, as of the May 2026 snapshot date, the fastest-growing design-in vertical VPG has encountered in its history as a standalone company. The company's growth initiatives program — targeting components for humanoid robot joints, AI infrastructure, defense, and advanced test-and-measurement — generated $37.8 million in orders in fiscal 2025, exceeding its $30 million internal target by 26%. Three separate developers had placed orders by early 2026. Whether that pipeline converts to production volumes at the scale robotics manufacturers have publicly projected is the central question this dossier examines.

The third is capital discipline. At December 31, 2025, VPG held $87.4 million in cash against only $20.6 million in long-term debt — a net cash position of approximately $66.8 million, equivalent to more than 20 cents per dollar of annual revenue. Total equity stood at $336.2 million across $455.9 million of assets. That balance sheet is not an accident; it is the result of fifteen years of conservative capital allocation under a chief executive who has run the company since its first day of trading.

## Scale, Context, and the Recovery Path

Revenue context matters here. [VPG's fiscal 2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001487952&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=10) reported full-year revenues of $307.2 million, essentially flat against $306.5 million in 2024 and materially below the $355.1 million peak recorded in fiscal 2023. The table below traces the contour of that cycle:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Gross Margin | Net Income (attributable) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2023 | $355.1 M | ~41% | — (peak year) |
| 2024 | $306.5 M | 41.0% | $9.9 M |
| 2025 | $307.2 M | 38.9% | $5.3 M |
| Q1 2026 | $84.4 M | 39.0% | — |

VPG is recovering, not yet at new highs. The $84.4 million Q1 2026 result — a 17.6% year-over-year acceleration — implies an annualized run rate approaching $335 million, still below 2023's peak. A structural step-up in humanoid robot demand is what transforms the recovery into something qualitatively different.

## The Human Through-Line

The biographical thread connecting Dr. Zandman's 1950s Paris laboratory to VPG's 2026 robotics strategy runs through Ziv Shoshani, Dr. Zandman's nephew and the company's President and Chief Executive Officer since the day trading began. Shoshani joined Vishay Intertechnology in 1995, rose through the capacitors and resistors businesses, served as Chief Operating Officer from 2007 to 2009, and was the designated steward of the Precision Group's independence from the moment the spin-off was announced. He understands the foil technology not as an acquired asset but as a family inheritance — which may partly explain why VPG has resisted the temptation to trade margin for growth in the way that larger industrial sensor peers sometimes have. The Zandman family, including Shoshani, retains approximately 35.1% of total voting power through Class B shares, ensuring that no acquirer can easily redirect the company's course.

## The Question the Dossier Will Try to Answer

The $102.1 million bookings quarter and the three humanoid robot design-in relationships are facts. What remains unanswered — and what the chapters that follow will examine from every angle available — is whether a company of VPG's scale, with this ownership structure and this manufacturing footprint, can convert a genuine first-mover position in humanoid robot sensing into a durable, multi-year revenue step-up. Or whether the bookings enthusiasm visible in early 2026 is a cyclical spike that will fade as larger, better-capitalized sensor competitors — with deeper pockets and broader distribution — sharpen their focus on the same joint-torque application and erode the design-in lead that VPG has spent five years quietly accumulating.

chapters.title: From Zandman's Wartime Physics to a NYSE Spinoff: VPG's Six Decades of Accumulated Precision
chapters.body:
## A Physicist's Obsession, Forged in Wartime

The technology at the core of Vishay Precision Group was not born in a corporate laboratory. It was born in a cellar.

Felix Zandman spent twenty-two months of the Second World War concealed beneath the floorboards of a Polish farmer's farmhouse in the Grodno region of what is today Belarus, one of a handful of Jews who survived the systematic liquidation of the surrounding communities. He emerged in 1944 into a world that had erased nearly everything familiar to him, including the village of Vishay in Lithuania where most of his family had perished. What he carried forward was an uncommon mind — mathematical, precise, obsessive about physical phenomena — and a determination to deploy it.

Zandman made his way to Paris, where he pursued graduate physics at the Sorbonne under the postwar intellectual ferment that had attracted the best European scientists who had survived the previous decade. His doctoral research drew him toward the behavior of metal alloys under stress, and in particular toward the optical and electrical phenomena that emerged when thin metallic films were strained. This was not casual curiosity. Zandman understood, at a level grounded in quantum mechanics, how electron transport through a crystalline metallic lattice responds to the mechanical deformation of the lattice itself — and he recognized that, if the composition of the alloy could be precisely controlled, the resulting conductive film would exhibit a temperature coefficient of resistance orders of magnitude lower than anything then commercially available.

The two inventions that followed from this insight defined what would eventually become VPG's technological identity. The first was PhotoStress®: a birefringent coating that, when applied to a loaded structure and illuminated with polarized light, revealed the full-field distribution of principal stresses across the surface — an analytical tool of tremendous value to structural engineers and, later, to aerospace designers validating airframe components. The second was Bulk Metal® Foil. Rather than winding resistance wire or depositing thick-film paste, Zandman etched a precision resistive element from a thin foil of a proprietary nickel-chromium alloy. The result was a resistor capable of temperature coefficients as low as ±0.2 parts per million per degree Celsius and load-life drift below 0.005% — specifications that commodity thick-film and wirewound alternatives have never matched, and which, as of the frozen window, they still cannot.

## Vishay Intertechnology: The Malvern Founding and the Acquisition Era

In 1962, Zandman incorporated Vishay Intertechnology, Inc. in Malvern, Pennsylvania, a township west of Philadelphia that would remain the company's address for the next six decades. The name was deliberate and mournful: Vishay for the Lithuanian village where his family died, rendered into the name of a company that would outlast all the forces that had tried to destroy him. The early product line was narrow — precision foil resistors sold primarily to aerospace contractors and defense electronics programs where stability across temperature extremes was a hard engineering requirement rather than a differentiating feature. The Pentagon and NASA were natural first customers; the reliability specifications they demanded in the 1960s were precisely the environment in which Bulk Metal® Foil held an unassailable advantage over every competing resistor technology.

The transformation from a single-product precision manufacturer into a diversified electronic components group began in earnest in the 1970s and accelerated through the 1980s and 1990s. Under Zandman's direction, Vishay Intertechnology executed a serial acquisition strategy of considerable ambition, purchasing dozens of components businesses across the United States, Europe, and Asia. The resulting conglomerate encompassed capacitors, inductors, diodes, transistors, and optoelectronics alongside its original resistor franchise — a portfolio that by the 2000s had made Vishay Intertechnology one of the largest diversified passive-components manufacturers in the world.

Within that structure, however, a distinct cluster of businesses was taking shape around the precision-measurement applications of the original foil technology. Micro-Measurements, the Wendell, North Carolina manufacturer of strain gauges used in experimental stress analysis, brought to Vishay a complementary sensor franchise with deep roots in aerospace structures testing, civil engineering, and geotechnical monitoring. KELK, based in Magog, Quebec, contributed tension, speed, and shape measurement systems designed for steel and aluminum rolling mills — a highly specialized metrology niche with long replacement cycles and deeply entrenched customer relationships. BLH Nobel, headquartered in Gothenburg, Sweden, added industrial weighing: load cells, force transducers, and platform scales used in food processing, crane and hoist applications, and general manufacturing. Stress-Tek, Pacific Instruments of West Warwick, Rhode Island, and Dynamic Systems Inc. of Poulsbo, Washington — the company behind the Gleeble thermal-mechanical simulation system used by metallurgists worldwide — each added further specialized measurement and data-acquisition capabilities that, taken individually, served narrow but defensible niches. Collectively, they constituted something more coherent: a precision-measurement platform with almost no overlap with Vishay Intertechnology's commodity-components businesses.

## The Spinoff Decision and the Architecture of Independence

By the late 2000s, the strategic mismatch between the Precision Group and the rest of Vishay Intertechnology had become difficult to ignore. The commodity components businesses — resistors, capacitors, diodes — competed on price, scale, and supply-chain efficiency. Margins were cyclical, inventory management was operationally intensive, and growth came from market-share capture in fragmented global markets. The Precision Group operated on an entirely different logic: long qualification cycles, application-specific engineering, premium pricing, and growth from expanding the scope of measurement applications rather than from volume displacement. Combining the two within a single capital allocation framework imposed costs on both.

In October 2009, Vishay Intertechnology's board announced its intention to spin off the Precision Group as a standalone public company. Ziv Shoshani, then serving as Vishay's Chief Operating Officer — and a nephew of Felix Zandman, who had joined the parent company in 1995 and risen through the capacitors and resistors businesses before assuming the COO role in January 2007 — was designated to lead the new entity through the preparation period and into its independent life. The structural separation involved carving out the foil resistors manufacturing operations in Dimona, Israel, the Micro-Measurements facility in Wendell, the KELK plant in Magog, and the various weighing and measurement systems operations, together with the intellectual property, customer relationships, and approximately 2,000 employees associated with them.

On July 6, 2010, Vishay Precision Group, Inc. began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker VPG, with approximately 13.3 million shares outstanding and three reporting segments — Foil Technology Products (subsequently renamed Sensors), Weighing Modules and Control Systems (subsequently Weighing Solutions), and Measurement Systems. The listing price and the separation agreement terms reflected an independent company that had been carefully prepared for standalone operation, not one hurriedly divested. Shoshani assumed the title of President and Chief Executive Officer from the first day of trading, a position he has held continuously through the frozen window date of May 23, 2026.

## Fifteen Years of Disciplined Accumulation

The acquisition strategy that Shoshani pursued as an independent CEO followed a markedly different pattern from the scale-driven rollups of Vishay Intertechnology's growth era. Each deal was small, technically complementary to an existing segment, and structured to avoid the leverage that had complicated several of the parent company's larger historical transactions. The acquisition of Dynamic Test Systems and the integration of Pacific Instruments deepened the Measurement Systems segment's signal-conditioning and data-acquisition capabilities without materially altering the balance sheet. The September 2024 purchase of Nokra Optische Prueftechnik & Automation GmbH — a Aachen-based developer of laser-based thickness, flatness, and 3D-profile gauging systems for metal rolling lines — for approximately EUR 3.95 million exemplified the approach at its most refined: a technically sophisticated product line, a specific cross-sell opportunity into KELK's existing mill-measurement customer base, and a transaction size that required no debt and no dilution.

> "Nokra offers customers a high-value alternative to existing technologies in the market," Shoshani said at the time of the announcement — a formulation that captured both the competitive positioning and the measured ambition characteristic of his M&A philosophy.

## An Organizational Capstone

The chapter that Zandman's wartime physics opened — and that Shoshani's fifteen years of institution-building continued — reached a structural inflection in November 2025, when VPG announced the creation of two C-suite positions that had never existed in the company's history. Yair Alcobi was appointed Chief Business and Product Officer, responsible for centralized product strategy across all three segments. Rafi Ouzan was named Chief Operating Officer, charged with standardizing execution across a manufacturing footprint that spans Israel, North America, Europe, and Asia. Management described the appointments as designed to "accelerate growth and standardize operations" — language that acknowledged, implicitly, that the operational infrastructure built to serve a $200 million revenue base required reinforcement before it could absorb the demand surge that humanoid robotics, AI infrastructure, and defense electronics were beginning to generate.

It was, in a sense, the logical endpoint of the arc that had begun in a Paris physics laboratory seven decades earlier: a company named for the dead of a Lithuanian village, built on the quantum mechanics of metal alloy conduction, now staffing itself to meet the demands of the machines that might one day walk among us.

chapters.title: Three Segments, One Foundational Material Science: VPG's Product Portfolio from Foil Resistors to Laser Mill Gauges
chapters.body:
## The Physics That Made Everything Else Possible

Understanding Vishay Precision Group's competitive position requires understanding one manufacturing process — a process elegant enough to fit on a single glass slide yet precise enough to satisfy the standards of the United States Department of Defense and the most demanding avionics integrators in the world.

Bulk Metal® Foil technology begins with a metal alloy — a proprietary blend of nickel, chromium, and other elements whose exact composition Dr. Felix Zandman refined through years of experimentation — that is rolled into a foil between eight and ten micrometers thick, roughly one-tenth the diameter of a human hair. That foil is then laminated onto a non-conductive ceramic or glass substrate, creating a blank from which the resistor geometry is subsequently carved. The carving is photolithographic: a light-sensitive resist is applied to the foil surface, a photomask defining the precise zigzag geometry of the resistor element is placed over it, and ultraviolet light exposes the pattern. Chemical etching removes the unmasked foil, leaving behind a serpentine metallic grid bonded firmly to its substrate.

The physics that follow from this construction are commercially significant in a way that took decades for the broader electronics industry to fully appreciate. Because the foil grid and its substrate are bonded across their entire interface — not merely at termination points as in wirewound resistors — the two expand and contract together as temperature changes. The alloy composition is tuned so that the mechanical stress induced by thermal expansion nearly exactly cancels the intrinsic change in the metal's resistivity, producing a temperature coefficient of resistance, or TCR, that can be held to less than ±0.2 parts per million per degree Celsius in VPG's most demanding variants. To put that in engineering context: across a temperature swing of 100 degrees Celsius — the kind of range an avionics system might traverse between a cold-soak ground start and sustained Mach-speed flight — a conventional thick-film resistor might drift by 100 to 200 parts per million. A Bulk Metal Foil resistor drifts by 20 parts per million or less.

The same construction principle suppresses long-term drift under electrical load. Because the foil grid is not under mechanical tension — it sits relaxed on its substrate — the microscopic grain-boundary creep that degrades wirewound and film elements over time is suppressed. VPG has published load-life stability data showing drift below 0.005% after 2,000 hours at rated power, a figure that most thick-film manufacturers cannot approach. This stability is not merely a marketing claim; it is the reason VPG's resistors survive incoming quality inspection at prime aerospace contractors who verify the specification independently.

## The Sensors Segment: Two Distinct Businesses, One Substrate

VPG's Sensors segment houses two product families that are related by manufacturing process but serve quite different commercial functions. Understanding the distinction is essential to reading the company's segment margins.

The first family is precision foil resistors, sold under the Vishay Foil Resistors brand and manufactured principally in Dimona, Israel. These are passive circuit components — elements whose purpose is to establish and maintain an accurate, stable resistance value within an electronic circuit. Applications range from the feedback networks inside avionics power supplies to the reference resistors in MRI gradient amplifiers to the signal-conditioning stages in fiber-optic line cards. For each of these uses, the customer is not measuring anything; it is relying on the resistor to hold a value without drifting. The most stringent variants — sub-0.2 ppm/°C TCR, hermetically sealed in welded metal cans for space qualification — command substantial price premiums and face essentially no commodity competition. Defense and aerospace contractors qualify these components through test programs that can run eighteen to twenty-four months; once a Vishay Foil Resistor is designed into a flight program, it remains in that program for the aircraft's operational life.

The second family is foil strain gauges, sold under the Micro-Measurements brand and manufactured in Wendell, North Carolina. These are transducer elements — thin metallic grids adhesively bonded to a structure under test, designed to convert mechanical strain into a change in electrical resistance that can be read by a Wheatstone bridge circuit. The physics are the same as in a precision resistor, but the application is the inverse: here, intentional bending of the foil grid under structural load is the signal. Standard laboratory-grade gauges serve stress analysts in automotive and aerospace structural testing; high-temperature variants rated for operation above 300 degrees Celsius serve turbine-blade and jet-engine test rigs. The PhotoStress® full-field instruments, another Zandman invention, extend strain analysis to entire surface areas by applying a birefringent coating to a test part and illuminating it with polarized light — each color fringe in the resulting image represents an iso-stress contour, allowing engineers to identify stress concentrations without instrumenting dozens of point locations.

Together, the Sensors segment generated $30.4 million in Q4 2025 revenue, implying a full-year run rate approaching $120 million. Industry observers and VPG management have consistently described this segment as carrying the company's highest gross margins, reflecting the Bulk Metal Foil IP premium and the long customer qualification cycles that limit price competition.

## Weighing Solutions: A Brand Portfolio in Industrial Load Measurement

The Weighing Solutions segment is structurally different from Sensors: it sells configured systems and subsystems to industrial end-users and OEMs rather than catalog components to circuit designers. Its brand architecture reflects decades of acquisitions by Vishay Intertechnology, each adding a specialized application niche.

VPG Transducers and Celtron form the general industrial backbone — single-point, shear-beam, and compression load cells for conveyor scales, hopper weighing, and factory automation, priced for cost-sensitive OEM customers integrating weighing capability into larger machines. BLH Nobel, with its Gothenburg, Sweden engineering base, occupies the high-accuracy tier: NTEP-certified systems for legal-for-trade applications, tank and silo weighing for the food, beverage, and chemical industries, and process weighing installations requiring hazardous-area certification. Stress-Tek targets crane and hoist manufacturers, providing force links and tension shackles that allow mobile cranes to display live hook load and protect against overloading — a regulatory requirement in most major markets. Vulcan's stainless-steel and hermetically sealed load cells serve washdown and outdoor harsh environments where standard industrial cells would corrode. VPG Onboard Weighing rounds out the segment with onboard axle-load monitoring systems for trucks, trailers, and rail wagons — a market sustained by European and Asian regulatory mandates requiring gross vehicle weight compliance at the point of loading rather than at fixed roadside checkpoints.

The commercial distinction between OEM and end-user channels matters for the segment's margin and cyclicality profile. OEM customers — machine builders who incorporate VPG load cells into larger equipment — demand competitive pricing, large volumes, and long-term supply agreements, compressing unit margins but providing revenue visibility. End-user and system-integrator customers buying complete BLH Nobel or Stress-Tek installations pay for application engineering, site commissioning, and compliance certification, generating higher per-unit revenue. The Weighing Solutions segment contributed approximately $27.7 million in Q4 2025 revenue, suggesting a full-year total in the range of $105 million.

## Measurement Systems: Three Distinct Franchises Under One Roof

The Measurement Systems segment is the most technically heterogeneous of VPG's three reporting units, and arguably the most interesting from an intellectual-property perspective, because it houses several franchises that each hold near-monopoly positions in their respective application niches.

KELK, based in Magog, Quebec, makes the tension, speed, and flatness measurement systems that steel and aluminum rolling mills rely upon to control strip shape and dimensional tolerances in real time. KELK's flatness systems use arrays of capacitive sensors to measure the crown and crossbow of rolled metal strip as it passes through the finishing mill at speeds exceeding 2,000 meters per minute — a non-contact measurement environment where any physical contact would damage both the strip and the sensor. The Nokra acquisition in September 2024, completed for approximately EUR 3.95 million, extended this capability into laser-based thickness and 3D-profile gauging using triangulation principles, allowing VPG to offer steel mill customers a single-vendor solution for inline dimensional metrology. The two franchises are being cross-sold into each other's installed base.

DSI's Gleeble thermal-mechanical simulation systems occupy a different application class entirely. A Gleeble machine subjects small metal specimens to precisely programmed combinations of electrical resistance heating — capable of reaching 3,000 degrees Celsius per second — and mechanical compression or tension, reproducing the thermomechanical history experienced by metal during industrial processing. Materials scientists use Gleeble systems to develop new alloy compositions, optimize rolling schedules, and study hot-ductility behavior without running full-scale mill trials. With more than 300 units installed at universities, national laboratories, and steel companies globally, the Gleeble franchise holds a position in academic metallurgy that no competitor has successfully challenged in decades.

Pacific Instruments contributes data acquisition hardware and signal conditioning modules used in test-and-measurement laboratories, and DTS (Dynamic Test Systems) provides compact ruggedized data recorders for crash-test and impact-testing programs in the automotive and military sectors.

The Measurement Systems segment generated $22.4 million in Q4 2025 revenue, for an implied full-year total of approximately $85 million, the smallest of the three segments. Its capital intensity is above average — KELK and Gleeble systems represent capital equipment purchases rather than consumable components — and its cyclicality tracks steel-industry capital expenditure, which introduces lumpiness into annual revenues.

| Segment | Q4 2025 Revenue | Implied FY2025 Run Rate | Primary End Markets | Margin Positioning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sensors | $30.4M | ~$118M | Defense, aerospace, robotics, T&M | Highest (Bulk Metal Foil IP premium) |
| Weighing Solutions | $27.7M | ~$105M | Industrial, food/bev, transportation | Mid (OEM price pressure vs. system margin) |
| Measurement Systems | $22.4M | ~$85M | Steel mills, materials research, defense test | Mid-to-low (capital equipment cyclicality) |

*Source: VPG Q4 2025 earnings release, 8-K filed with SEC EDGAR; full-year estimates are proportional extrapolations.*

## The Robot Joint: Where Foil Technology Finds Its Newest Market

The most consequential application for Bulk Metal Foil technology in 2025 and 2026 was not a military radar system or an MRI scanner. It was the torque sensor embedded in the knee joint of a humanoid robot.

Joint-torque sensing is the mechanism by which a robot achieves proprioception — the sense, analogous to the human nervous system's feedback from muscles and tendons, of how much force is being exerted at each joint and in what direction. Without accurate joint-torque measurement, a bipedal robot cannot reliably modulate the force of its steps, respond gracefully to unexpected contact with obstacles, or perform manipulation tasks requiring delicate force control. Achieving proprioception demands a force transducer that is simultaneously compact enough to fit inside a robot joint housing, precise enough to detect millinewton-meter torque variations, fatigue-resistant enough to survive millions of load cycles without drift, and stable enough across the temperature range of an operating robot that its readings do not require continuous recalibration.

VPG's foil strain gauges meet each of these constraints in ways that alternative technologies — semiconductor piezoresistive gauges, magnetostrictive sensors, optical fiber Bragg gratings — do not simultaneously achieve. The Bulk Metal Foil gauge can be configured as a rosette — a multi-axis pattern etched from a single foil blank — bonded directly to a machined metal flexure element within the joint. The resulting transducer package can measure torque in multiple axes, withstand millions of fatigue cycles with drift below the instrument's measurement threshold, and operate without recalibration across the 0–60 degree Celsius skin-temperature range of a working robot.

Management commentary during 2025 earnings calls documented the commercial progress: a lead humanoid robot developer progressed to pre-production orders, a second placed prototype orders in Q4 2025, and a third entered the design-in pipeline by January 2026. VPG's growth-initiatives bookings program — which includes humanoid robotics alongside AI data-center power management and defense electronics — generated $37.8 million in orders for full-year 2025, exceeding the company's $30 million internal target by 26%. While VPG has not publicly disclosed a per-robot sensor content value, analysts covering the robotics sensor supply chain have estimated that a fully instrumented humanoid platform incorporating joint-torque sensors, force-sensitive end-effectors, and structural strain monitoring could require between $200 and $500 in precision sensor content per unit, depending on the number of articulated degrees of freedom. At the mid-point of that range, a production run of 50,000 humanoid robots — a figure consistent with publicly stated ambitions of several developers for the 2027–2028 timeframe — would represent a demand increment of approximately $17.5 million annually, equivalent to roughly 15% of the Sensors segment's current revenue base. The inflection, in other words, would not merely be additive; at scale, it could define the segment's growth trajectory for the better part of a decade.

The company opened the decade in mild contraction, with 2016 revenues of $225 million reflecting a broad softening in global industrial spending. The recovery through 2017 and into 2018 — when revenues touched $300 million for the first time — tracked a synchronised global industrial expansion and a defence electronics procurement cycle that amplified demand for precision foil resistors and strain gauges. That $300 million threshold proved a ceiling, not a floor: the 2019 industrial cycle deceleration and the COVID-related disruption of 2020 combined to pull revenues back to $270 million, a two-year retracement of 10% that exposed the limits of VPG's pricing power when volume declines.

The post-COVID rebound was the sharpest in the company's public-market history. Revenues rose 17.8% in 2021 and a further 14.2% in 2022, cresting at $363 million, as deferred capital spending in steel processing, defence re-arming, and advanced test-and-measurement applications simultaneously reversed. The 2023 figure of $355.1 million represented the post-COVID high-water mark, followed by a sharp $48.6 million contraction in 2024 — the deepest single-year revenue decline since the spinoff — as industrial customers burned down inflated inventories of load cells and weighing modules accumulated during the supply-chain-crisis era. Full-year 2025 revenues of $307.2 million were essentially unchanged from $306.5 million in 2024, suggesting the inventory digestion cycle had run its course but that a genuine volume recovery had not yet arrived. That recovery was, by the snapshot date, in motion: the fiscal Q1 2026 result of $84.4 million implied an annualised run rate of approximately $337 million, with Q2 2026 guidance of $85–$90 million pointing toward a modest but real upswing.

## Margin Anatomy: The 38–42% Corridor and Its Discontents

VPG's gross margin corridor — 38 to 42 percent over the full business cycle — is the fingerprint of a precision-niche manufacturer rather than a commodity component supplier. Achieving and sustaining margins in that range on a $307 million revenue base requires consistent pricing power against customers who are engineering-constrained rather than cost-constrained, and VPG has consistently demonstrated that power in its Sensors segment, where Bulk Metal® Foil resistors command premiums that commodity thin-film and wirewound alternatives cannot erode.

The 2024 gross margin of 41.0 percent represented the cycle peak — a combination of post-COVID pricing gains, favourable product mix toward higher-value Sensors revenue, and the tail end of supply-side constraints that had reduced competitive pressure. The compression to 38.9 percent in full-year 2025 reflected two converging forces. First, revenue mix shifted adversely: the Measurement Systems segment, which carries lower gross margins on its project-oriented mill-gauging contracts, grew proportionally as several large steel-industry orders were recognised. Sensors revenue, the margin engine, remained stable but did not expand enough to offset the mix drag. Second, Q4 2025 exposed the operating-leverage vulnerability of a $300 million business: with revenues of $80.6 million and a fixed manufacturing cost base spread across facilities in Malvern (Pennsylvania), Wendell (North Carolina), Dimona (Israel), and Chennai (India), the quarterly gross margin fell to 36.8 percent.

> "The Q4 gross margin was impacted by approximately $1 million of unfavourable product mix and $1 million from inventory reduction," CEO Ziv Shoshani said on the Q4 2025 earnings call.

Those two line items — roughly $2 million of combined headwind on an $80.6 million revenue base — illustrate how thin the margin cushion becomes at the trough. The partial recovery to 39.0 percent in Q1 2026, as revenue reached $84.4 million and Sensors bookings surged on robotics and defence demand, confirmed the operating-leverage dynamic in the opposite direction: incremental revenue at the Sensors margin rate flows through to gross profit disproportionately.

Currency effects compound the complexity. The Israeli shekel and Indian rupee affect manufacturing costs at two of VPG's largest production sites. The company does not provide detailed currency-attribution in its margin disclosures, but the Israel-based foil-resistor facility's cost base introduces meaningful shekel exposure that management partially hedges.

## The GAAP-to-Adjusted EBITDA Bridge

The gap between VPG's 4.5 percent GAAP operating margin and its 9.2 percent adjusted EBITDA margin in 2025 tells the story of the company's acquisition-built history. On $307.2 million in revenue, the 470-basis-point spread between those two figures amounts to roughly $14 million in adjustments — the quantitative legacy of a fifteen-year programme of bolt-on acquisitions that left the income statement encumbered with amortisation charges on acquired intangibles.

Adjusted EBITDA of $28.2 million absorbed back the principal non-cash and non-recurring items: amortisation of intangibles acquired through deals including BLH Nobel, KELK, DSI, and Nokra; depreciation on manufacturing plant and equipment; restructuring charges associated with workforce and facility adjustments; and stock-based compensation for executives and directors. Net earnings attributable to VPG stockholders fell to $5.3 million, or $0.40 per diluted share, from $9.9 million, or $0.74 per diluted share, in 2024 — a decline of 46.5 percent that triggered complete forfeiture of performance-based cash bonuses and the vesting of 2023-vintage performance restricted stock units, as reported in the [2026 DEF 14A proxy statement filed with the SEC](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001487952&type=DEF+14A).

Management's long-term model targets double-digit adjusted EBITDA margins as revenue scales toward $400 million. The path to that target runs through the $6 million in annualised cost reductions identified for fiscal 2026, driven by manufacturing efficiency programmes and overhead consolidation following the appointment of a Chief Operating Officer in November 2025. If those savings are realised in full and flow to EBITDA without reinvestment drag, the 2026 adjusted EBITDA margin on a $335 million revenue run-rate would approach approximately 11 percent — materially above the 2025 result and within range of the management model. The caveat is that a portion of those savings may be partially reinvested in robotics-specific production capacity at the Wendell strain-gauge facility and the Dimona foil-resistor plant.

## The Balance Sheet: Net Cash as Strategic Optionality

At December 31, 2025, VPG's balance sheet presented a picture unusual among industrial sensor manufacturers of similar revenue scale. Cash and equivalents of $87.4 million stood against long-term debt of only $20.6 million, yielding a net cash position of $66.8 million — equivalent to 21.7 cents of net cash per dollar of annual revenue, and more than 14.6 percent of total assets of $455.9 million.

| Balance Sheet Item | Dec 31, 2025 |
|---|---|
| Cash & equivalents | $87.4M |
| Long-term debt | $20.6M |
| Net cash | $66.8M |
| Total equity | $336.2M |
| Total assets | $455.9M |

The debt reduction of approximately $10.8 million from the prior year-end balance of $31.4 million reflected scheduled amortisation and optional prepayments, consistent with management's longstanding preference for a conservative leverage profile. The remaining assets comprise primarily acquired goodwill and intangibles from the M&A programme — a material item given the prices paid for BLH Nobel, KELK, DSI, and Nokra relative to their tangible book values — along with manufacturing PP&E and trade receivables. The goodwill and intangibles burden represents a genuine risk factor: in a severe revenue downturn, the carrying values of these assets could face impairment testing pressure that would flow through to reported equity.

Total equity of $336.2 million against $455.9 million in total assets implies an equity-to-assets ratio of approximately 73.7 percent — a balance-sheet structure that leaves VPG with ample capacity for bolt-on M&A without recourse to dilutive equity issuance, as demonstrated by the September 2024 acquisition of Nokra for approximately EUR 3.95 million, funded from existing cash resources.

## Cash Generation and the Cost-Reduction Dividend

Operating cash flow of $14.4 million and adjusted free cash flow of $17.3 million in 2025 were modest against the revenue base — an FCF margin of approximately 5.6 percent — but consistent with a margin-compressed trough year in which working capital absorbed some of the headwind. Capital expenditures were modest, reflecting the company's relatively asset-light manufacturing model in precision components: foil-resistor production is capital-light relative to silicon-based semiconductor fabrication, and the primary capex requirement is tooling and equipment upgrades rather than new-line construction.

The $6 million in targeted cost reductions for 2026, if fully delivered, would represent a cash earnings uplift of roughly 42 percent above the 2025 adjusted free cash flow level — a significant step-up on a $17.3 million base. Management has not disclosed the precise composition of those savings, but the appointment of Chief Operating Officer Rafi Ouzan suggests that procurement consolidation, manufacturing process standardisation, and back-office rationalisation across the multi-site global footprint are the principal levers.

## The Re-Rating: Robotics Optionality Meets Cyclical Recovery

The most striking financial development in VPG's recent history has been valuation. At the 10-K's reference price date of June 27, 2025, 13.3 million shares outstanding at approximately $26 per share produced a market capitalisation of $346.8 million. Subtracting the net cash position of $66.8 million yields an enterprise value of approximately $280 million at that date. On trailing 2025 revenues of $307.2 million and adjusted EBITDA of $28.2 million, the implied multiples were roughly 0.91x EV/Revenue and 9.9x EV/EBITDA — cheap for a precision-niche manufacturer with a genuine technological moat, but reflective of the earnings trough and investor scepticism about the robotics opportunity's near-term commercialisation timeline.

| Valuation Scenario | Share Price | Market Cap | EV | EV/Revenue | EV/EBITDA |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mid-2025 (trough) | ~$26 | ~$346M | ~$280M | ~0.91x | ~9.9x |
| Early 2026 (re-rated) | ~$47–$50 | ~$620–$640M | ~$555–$575M | ~1.8x | ~19.8x |

By early calendar 2026, the stock had roughly doubled. At $48 per share, the market capitalisation approximated $638 million, implying an enterprise value of approximately $571 million — 1.86x trailing revenues and approximately 20.2x trailing adjusted EBITDA. That re-rating embedded both a cyclical earnings recovery expectation (consensus pointing toward 2026 revenues of $335–$355 million and margin improvement from the cost programme) and a robotics-optionality premium that the prior multiple had not priced.

Mettler-Toledo, the nearest large-cap peer at approximately $3.7 billion in revenue and an $18 billion market capitalisation, commands approximately 4.9x EV/Revenue — a level VPG is nowhere near, but one that illustrates the ceiling the market would assign if the robotics thesis fully materialised at scale. HBK, the private Spectris-owned precision measurement franchise at roughly $1.3 billion in revenue, trades at an implied multiple in the 2.5–3.0x EV/Revenue range based on Spectris's disclosed segment economics. VPG's post-re-rating multiple of approximately 1.86x EV/Revenue sits meaningfully below both comparables, suggesting that the market is pricing partial but not full delivery of the robotics volume ramp — a reasonable discount given that humanoid robot production at scale remains, as of the snapshot date, a 2026–2028 event horizon rather than a current-quarter revenue line.

The arithmetic of the re-rating points to a market that has made a bet: that VPG's Q1 2026 bookings milestone of $102.1 million, its $37.8 million in growth-initiative orders in 2025, and its book-to-bill of 1.21 are leading indicators of a revenue trajectory that exits the $307 million trough and begins a climb toward the $400 million management model target — with robotics design-in wins converting from prototype orders to production contracts as humanoid robot developers enter commercial deployment. Whether that bet pays off hinges on execution, on the pace of robot commercialisation, and on whether VPG's balance sheet discipline — the net-cash fortress that Shoshani has maintained through fifteen years of cycle volatility — proves sufficient to fund the capacity additions the demand inflection will require.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Tale of Two Multiples

Vishay Precision Group entered fiscal 2026 as a different stock than the one that filed its fiscal 2024 annual report. Between the 10-K reference price date of June 27, 2025 — when the company's market capitalization stood at approximately $346.8 million, implying roughly $26 per share across 13.3 million diluted shares — and the frozen snapshot window of May 2026, the stock had approximately doubled to a market capitalization in the $615–$640 million range. No single quarterly earnings release drove that re-rating. Instead, it accumulated through a sequence of signals: $37.8 million in growth-initiative bookings against a $30 million target, a second humanoid robotics developer ordering prototypes, a third placing initial orders, and then the first $100 million quarterly bookings milestone in Q1 2026. The valuation question worth answering is whether the re-rating is finished or whether the current price still embeds a meaningful discount to intrinsic value — and, equally, where the price is vulnerable if the robotics narrative stalls.

## Current Multiples: The Arithmetic

Using an estimated market capitalization of approximately $625 million as of mid-May 2026 — derived from the reported 13.3 million diluted shares multiplied by a price consistent with the "approximately doubled" description applied to early-2026 trading — and netting out VPG's $87.4 million cash position against $20.6 million in long-term debt, enterprise value stands at roughly $557 million.

Against fiscal 2025 trailing revenue of $307.2 million, that implies a trailing EV/Sales ratio of approximately **1.8x**. Against fiscal 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $28.2 million, the trailing EV/EBITDA multiple is approximately **19.7x** — elevated by the margin trough year. GAAP net income of $5.3 million and diluted EPS of $0.40 render the trailing P/E ratio of roughly **115x** analytically meaningless rather than alarming; the figure reflects an earnings base compressed by product-mix headwinds, inventory adjustments, and $6 million in annualized cost-reduction spending not yet fully annualizing through the income statement rather than a structurally impaired business. Price-to-book, at approximately $336.2 million in total equity, comes to approximately **1.9x** — modest for a specialty-technology franchise with genuine IP moat.

Forward estimates carry more signal. With Q1 2026 revenue of $84.4 million (implying roughly a $337 million run rate) and Q2 2026 guidance of $85–$90 million, a reasonable fiscal 2026 revenue estimate sits in the $340–$350 million range. If management's targeted cost savings close at least two-thirds by year-end, EBITDA margins should recover toward 11–12% — producing forward EBITDA in the $37–$42 million range. That implies a forward EV/EBITDA of approximately **13–15x**, a more digestible figure that begins to converge with industrial instrumentation peers. Forward P/E, assuming net income normalizes toward $12–$15 million on lower interest offsets and operational leverage, implies a forward earnings multiple of approximately **42–52x** — still a premium valuation, but one that reflects embedded optionality rather than current earnings power alone.

## Historical Multiple Range

At the June 2025 reference price, VPG traded at an EV/Sales multiple below 1.0x and an EV/EBITDA near 9–10x on trailing 2024 figures (when revenue was $306.5 million and EBITDA was somewhat higher than in 2025 given the 41.0% gross margin). That trough multiple was not unusual in the company's post-spinoff history. [SEC EDGAR VPG 10-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001487952&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=10) show that through most of the 2017–2021 period — when annual revenues oscillated between $225 million and $285 million and the robotics thesis did not exist — VPG traded at EV/Sales below 1.0x and EV/EBITDA in the 8–12x range, consistent with a capital-light industrial component company with limited revenue growth and no obvious secular tailwind. The 2022–2023 industrial boom pushed the stock to perhaps 14–16x EBITDA at the 2023 revenue peak of $355.1 million. The subsequent correction — reflecting both the industrial downcycle and investor skepticism that the robotics design-in wins would convert to volume production — compressed the multiple back toward the historical floor. The re-rating that followed is therefore not simply cyclical recovery: it represents a genuine narrative shift, from "precision-niche industrial components" to "mandatory supplier for humanoid robot proprioception," a framing that commands a structurally higher earnings multiple because it implies a steeper long-duration growth path.

## Peer-Group Comparison

VPG's closest public comparators span precision instruments, specialty sensors, and motion-technology components. The following table uses approximate multiples as of mid-2026, sourced from publicly available market data and company filings, and should be read as directional rather than precisely contemporaneous.

| Company | Ticker | EV/Sales | EV/EBITDA (Fwd) | Forward P/E | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vishay Precision Group | VPG | ~1.8x | ~14x | ~45x | Robotics re-rating; trough EBITDA base; net-cash balance sheet |
| Mettler-Toledo Intl | MTD | ~4.8x | ~22x | ~25x | Premium precision weighing/lab instruments; high recurring service revenue |
| Cognex | CGNX | ~5.5x | ~28x | ~35x | Machine-vision pure-play; higher gross margins (~75%); software component |
| Novanta | NOVT | ~4.5x | ~24x | ~38x | Precision motion & sensing for robotics/medtech; comparable growth narrative |
| Ametek | AME | ~4.2x | ~17x | ~22x | Diversified precision instruments; large scale; M&A compounder |
| Spectris (HBK parent) | SXS LN | ~2.0x | ~13x | ~19x | UK-listed instruments holding co.; includes VPG's most direct test-and-measurement rival |

VPG trades at a material discount to Cognex and Novanta on revenue and EBITDA multiples, which is defensible given VPG's smaller scale, lower gross margins (38–41% versus Cognex's 70%+), and still-unproven volume ramp. The discount to Mettler-Toledo and Ametek reflects the latter companies' far larger revenue bases, diversified product portfolios, and proven earnings compounding records. The comparison to Spectris is the most instructive: at roughly 2.0x EV/Sales, Spectris — which owns HBK, VPG's closest direct analog in precision test and measurement — trades broadly in line with VPG on a revenue multiple basis, suggesting the current VPG valuation embeds a robotics option premium above what a pure industrial peer would command.

## Intrinsic Value: What the Price Implies

A simplified discounted-cash-flow framing helps bracket the current price. Assume a cost of equity of approximately 9–10%, reflecting VPG's beta above 1.0 (a small-cap industrial with idiosyncratic robotics exposure), a net-cash balance sheet that reduces financial risk, and a terminal growth rate of 3.5% (consistent with long-run industrial GDP-plus growth). With fiscal 2025 adjusted free cash flow of $17.3 million and a current enterprise value of ~$557 million, the market is implying — working backward — that free cash flow must grow at roughly 12–15% compounded for at least eight to ten years before converging to a terminal rate. That is not a demanding assumption if the robotics ramp materializes: if Sensors revenue doubles over five years from roughly $100 million today to $200 million, and if the resulting incremental revenue flows through at operating margins above the current segment average, free cash flow could reach $45–$55 million by 2030 without straining any particularly aggressive modeling assumption. Conversely, if robotics bookings plateau and the Sensors segment reverts to its pre-2025 trajectory, the terminal cash-flow math justifies a market cap closer to $350–$400 million — implying the current stock embeds $200–$250 million of option value that must be earned through confirmed production volume.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — target: $88–$100 per share.** Humanoid robotics transitions from design-in to early production at two to three customers between 2026 and 2028. VPG's Sensors segment exits fiscal 2028 at $190–$210 million in annual revenue, and total company revenue reaches $430–$450 million. EBITDA margins expand to 14–15% on operating leverage from the fixed manufacturing cost base in Israel and North Carolina. At a 20–22x EV/EBITDA on $63–$68 million in EBITDA, enterprise value approaches $1.3–$1.5 billion; adding net cash and dividing by 13.3 million shares produces an equity value of $97–$117 per share. This requires no step-change acquisition, only execution on design-ins already underway.

**Base case — target: $55–$65 per share.** Industrial recovery continues at a measured pace. Robotics contributes meaningfully but remains sub-$50 million in annual Sensors revenue by fiscal 2027. Total company revenue reaches $365–$380 million by fiscal 2027, EBITDA margins recover to 11–12%, producing EBITDA of $40–$46 million. At a 15–17x EV/EBITDA multiple — consistent with a quality-but-cyclical precision instruments compounder — enterprise value is $600–$782 million; equity value runs $50–$64 per share. Modest upside from current levels, with downside protection provided by the net-cash position.

**Bear case — target: $34–$40 per share.** Robotics bookings convert slowly to revenue, the industrial cycle turns down again in late 2026, and margin recovery stalls at 9–10% EBITDA. Revenue flatlines near $325 million. At a 10–12x trough EV/EBITDA on $30–$33 million of EBITDA — roughly where the stock traded in mid-2025 before the robotics thesis crystallized — enterprise value is $300–$396 million; equity value is $27–$35 per share plus the $67 million net cash buffer, approximately $34–$40 per share. The floor is partially supported by the balance sheet itself.

## What the Market Is Pricing In — and the Gap

The current multiple tells a specific story: the market believes VPG is no longer a $300 million revenue company trading at an industrial trough multiple, but it has not yet granted it the full robotics-compounder premium that a company like Novanta commands. The gap between the base and bull cases — roughly $30–$40 per share, or 50–75% of current equity value — is the market's agnosticism about whether VPG's three humanoid robotics design-ins represent the first wave of a structural volume ramp or a wave of prototype-stage bookings that may take years to monetize at scale. The dossier's read is that the asymmetry favors the upside: with $102.1 million in Q1 2026 bookings, a book-to-bill of 1.21, a net-cash balance sheet that can fund capacity additions without dilution, and a technological moat in Bulk Metal® Foil that no announced competitor has replicated in the robotics sensing application, the conditions for multiple re-expansion into the bull-case range are present. The principal risk is time — specifically, whether humanoid robot production volume accelerates on the 2026–2028 timetable that venture-backed developers have projected, or whether the commercial ramp slips into 2028–2030 and the current premium reverts to a waiting-discount.

chapters.title: Quarter by Quarter: How Management Narrative and Bookings Data Have Told VPG's Robotics Story to the Market
chapters.body:
## The Cyclical Trough as Backdrop

For most of 2024, Vishay Precision Group was a story the market understood too well: a precision sensor manufacturer working through the downstream effects of a post-COVID capital-expenditure hangover in industrial weighing and measurement systems. Full-year 2024 revenues came in at $306.5 million — down sharply from the $355.1 million peak of fiscal 2023, a contraction of nearly 14% that tracked the familiar correction cycle in steel-mill investment and industrial logistics. Gross margin held at a respectable 41.0%, the highest in recent memory, and the balance sheet remained a point of institutional pride, with cash accumulating and long-term debt declining. But the headline revenue number, and the implicit message it carried about demand in VPG's core industrial end markets, kept the investment narrative anchored in cyclical recovery framing rather than structural re-rating. That would begin to change in the back half of 2024 — and accelerate, dramatically, through fiscal 2025.

## When Robotics Entered the Room

The precise timing of management's first public disclosure of humanoid robotics as a strategic growth theme cannot be pinned to a single earnings event without access to the full archive of call transcripts, but the contours are traceable through the bookings data and the language pattern that Shoshani adopted in successive quarters. The framework VPG constructed was the "growth initiatives" program — a defined, explicitly tracked basket of incremental bookings across four high-conviction end markets: humanoid robot joint-force sensors, AI data-center power-management components, defense electronics, and advanced test-and-measurement applications. By setting a public $30 million bookings target for these initiatives in fiscal 2025, management forced investors to hold management accountable on a concrete, measurable metric rather than a directional aspiration.

The language evolution across quarters was deliberate. In early 2025 quarters, Shoshani's framing was exploratory: VPG was in discussions with humanoid robot developers, prototypes were being evaluated, design-in timelines were uncertain. By mid-2025, with one lead customer having progressed to pre-production orders, the register shifted. By the Q3 2025 call, the tone had turned confirmatory. And when the full-year numbers were tallied — $37.8 million in growth-initiative bookings, exceeding the $30 million target by 26% — Shoshani could state plainly that VPG had exceeded its commitment. The progression from speculative to substantiated, quarter by quarter, is precisely the kind of narrative management credibility that institutional investors price into multiple expansion.

## The Q4 2025 Earnings Shock and What It Concealed

The market's reaction to Vishay Precision Group's fourth-quarter 2025 earnings announcement was swift and punishing. The stock fell 13.36% in a single session — a move that, on a company with a market capitalization then approaching $600 million, erased tens of millions of dollars in equity value in hours. The sell-off reflected three specific disappointments that arrived simultaneously.

First, gross margin came in at 36.8% for the quarter — the lowest reading in the recent fiscal record, and materially below the 41.0% the company had delivered for full-year 2024. The sequential deterioration of roughly 420 basis points from the prior-year period raised questions about pricing discipline, product mix, and the cost absorption capacity of VPG's manufacturing base. Second, the full-year 2025 net earnings of $5.3 million ($0.40 per diluted share) compared poorly to $9.9 million ($0.74 per diluted share) in 2024 — a 46% decline in reported profit against essentially flat revenues of $307.2 million, a combination that is particularly unattractive to earnings-oriented institutional holders. Third, the Q1 2026 guidance range of $74 million to $80 million (on a constant-currency basis) read as conservative at best, and at worst as a signal that the robotics-driven bookings momentum was not yet translating into recognizable revenue.

What the sell-off obscured, however, was a set of forward-looking signals that told a starkly different story. The overall Q4 2025 book-to-bill ratio was 1.01 — orders slightly exceeding shipments — and the Sensors segment, VPG's highest-margin business and the direct conduit for humanoid robotics demand, posted a 1.15 book-to-bill. The divergence between the GAAP earnings optics and the bookings trajectory illustrated a structural tension inherent in the design-in business model: the cost of building prototype capacity, qualifying new customers, and absorbing the engineering burden of the first humanoid robot applications flows through the income statement immediately, while the revenue benefit of those design-wins is deferred until customers reach volume production.

| Metric | Q4 2024 | Q4 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | ~$76M (est.) | $80.6M | +6% approx. |
| Gross margin | ~40%+ | 36.8% | –~320 bps |
| Net income per share | ~$0.25 (est.) | Negative YoY | — |
| Book-to-bill (Overall) | — | 1.01 | — |
| Book-to-bill (Sensors) | — | 1.15 | — |

## Q1 2026: The Vindication Quarter

The market's negative verdict on Q4 2025 lasted precisely one quarter. When VPG reported fiscal Q1 2026 results on May 12, 2026, the magnitude of the beat against the conservative guidance range was sufficient to reverse the narrative entirely. Revenue of $84.4 million — against a guided range of $74 million to $80 million — represented a 17.6% year-over-year acceleration and the strongest quarterly revenue in at least two years. More striking still, total bookings reached $102.1 million, producing a book-to-bill of 1.21 and marking the first time in company history that a single quarter had generated more than $100 million in orders.

Gross margin recovered to 39.0%, a sequential improvement of 220 basis points from Q4 2025's trough, and management attributed the expansion to improved product mix, the early benefits of targeted cost actions, and the higher-margin character of the Sensors segment's growing robotics and defense bookings. For Q2 2026, Shoshani issued guidance of $85 million to $90 million — a range that implied continued sequential growth and placed full-year 2026 on a trajectory to approach, if not surpass, the $355.1 million peak of fiscal 2023.

On the Q1 2026 earnings call, Shoshani surveyed the demand environment with a specificity that reflected the cumulative progress of the growth-initiatives program. He cited AI infrastructure, defense procurement, data centers, and humanoid robotics as the primary drivers of the $102.1 million bookings result. The stock responded positively — a direct inversion of the Q4 2025 reaction — as investors reconciled the conservative guidance cadence management had adopted with the underlying demand strength that the bookings data had been signaling for two consecutive quarters.

## The Compensation Paradox: Discipline as a Double-Edged Sword

Beneath the earnings narrative runs a compensation story that reveals something important about the tension between VPG's investment posture and its near-term earnings capacity. For fiscal 2025, the Compensation Committee measured performance against two primary annual incentive metrics: adjusted EBITDA of $54.3 million as target, and adjusted operating income of $25.5 million as target. Against those benchmarks, the company delivered adjusted EBITDA of $28.2 million — 51.9% of target — and adjusted operating income of $11.2 million, equating to 43.9% of target. Both figures fell below the threshold levels required to trigger any payout under the annual cash incentive plan.

The outcome: zero payout on performance-based annual cash bonuses for all named executive officers, including Shoshani. The 2023-vintage performance RSU tranche, which was also tied to multi-year financial metrics, similarly vested at zero. The proxy's disclosure of these outcomes was as unsparing as the structure itself:

> *Performance-based annual cash bonus: 0% payout. Performance RSU tranche (2023 grant): 0% vested.*

The rigor of that disclosure cuts two ways. On one hand, it signals precisely the kind of pay-for-performance alignment that institutional governance frameworks prescribe, and it reinforces management's stated commitment to accountability. On the other hand, it surfaces a genuine tension: the capital and organizational investment required to win humanoid robotics design-ins — prototype manufacturing, application engineering, customer qualification cycles that can span twelve to eighteen months — depresses the adjusted operating income and EBITDA metrics on which near-term compensation depends, even as it builds the design-in pipeline from which future revenue growth will be drawn. Executives at VPG were, in effect, investing in the company's five-year positioning while being compensated — or not compensated — on a one-year outcome.

That tension is not unique to VPG, but it is unusually visible here. The $37.8 million in growth-initiative bookings that management exceeded in 2025 will translate into recognized revenue across 2026 and beyond. The adjusted EBITDA that those bookings will eventually generate will fund future bonus pools and vest future RSU tranches. Whether the compensation architecture rewards the architects of that pipeline in proportion to the value they created — or whether it simply penalizes the transition period before the robotics revenues mature — is a question the board and incoming CFO successor to William Clancy will need to revisit as VPG scales toward its long-term $400 million revenue ambition.

chapters.title: The Founder's Nephew, a Departing CFO, and a Newly Built C-Suite: VPG's Leadership at a Pivotal Transition
chapters.body:
## The Founder's Nephew at the Helm

When Vishay Precision Group began trading on the New York Stock Exchange on July 6, 2010, its president and chief executive was a man who had spent the previous fifteen years inside Vishay Intertechnology learning, from the inside out, what made Bulk Metal® Foil technology commercially irreplaceable. Ziv Shoshani was also Dr. Felix Zandman's nephew — a biographical detail that is neither incidental nor, by itself, sufficient explanation for why he was the right person to lead the spinoff. What mattered was the combination: family proximity to the founding intelligence, and three decades of operational immersion that produced an executive who could discuss foil resistor metallurgy with engineers, negotiate acquisitions with targets, and speak to institutional investors about measurement precision as a competitive moat.

Shoshani joined Vishay Intertechnology in 1995 and rose through progressively senior roles — Executive Vice President of the Capacitors and Resistors businesses from 2000 to 2006, Deputy COO in 2006, and Chief Operating Officer from January 2007 through late 2009. The COO tenure was formative: he oversaw the operational architecture of a company generating several billion dollars in revenue across commodity and specialty electronic components, and he was managing the precision segment's distinct manufacturing culture — centered on the Dimona, Israel facility that Dr. Zandman had established — from within a much larger corporate parent. When Vishay's board announced the spinoff in October 2009, Shoshani's designation as the standalone company's CEO was institutional logic as much as family succession: no one else in the organization combined his knowledge of the foil IP, the Israeli manufacturing relationships, and the global sensor customer base.

The hereditary dimension of this leadership model carries genuine governance complexity. The case for it is alignment: a CEO whose family name is functionally synonymous with the company's founding technology has incentives that are measured in decades, not quarters. The case against it is the mirror image of the same fact — succession concentration, the risk of institutional memory residing in a single individual, and the absence of an obvious internal candidate to carry forward the organization if Shoshani were to depart unexpectedly. [VPG's 2026 proxy statement](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001487952/000143774926016226/ex_924354.htm) does not disclose a formal CEO succession plan, a disclosure gap that is common among founder-heritage companies but notable given the bookings inflection underway.

## The Architect of the Capital Structure

For as long as Shoshani has held the CEO seat, William M. Clancy has held the CFO's chair. Appointed Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer at the spinoff, Clancy built the financial architecture of VPG from the ground up: establishing the credit facility, underwriting the acquisitions — BLH Nobel, KELK, Pacific Instruments, DSI, and most recently Nokra for approximately EUR 3.95 million in September 2024 — and managing the investor relations posture through cycles of margin compression and recovery. Across fifteen years, he accumulated an institutional knowledge of VPG's balance sheet that is difficult to replicate quickly. The company entered fiscal 2026 with $87.4 million in cash, only $20.6 million of long-term debt, and a book-to-bill ratio of 1.21 on quarterly bookings of $102.1 million — its strongest demand environment as a public company.

Clancy's announced retirement, effective December 31, 2026, is therefore the most consequential near-term leadership event in VPG's history. The board initiated a search for his successor in early 2026, but the timing is structurally difficult: any incoming CFO will be learning the company's financial architecture — its multi-currency exposure across Israeli shekel, euro, and Canadian dollar operations, its acquisition underwriting discipline, and its investor communications approach — precisely as the robotics bookings acceleration demands sophisticated capital allocation decisions. The ideal successor profile is narrow: industry familiarity with precision sensor M&A, comfort with a sub-$400 million revenue base that may be entering a re-rating moment, and the investor relations sophistication to communicate the humanoid robotics thesis to a market that is simultaneously excited about the application and skeptical of small-cap execution. If the CFO search extends into the second half of 2026 without resolution, the transition risk compounds: Clancy would be managing year-end financial close and investor communications while simultaneously offboarding, a scenario that tests any organization's continuity planning.

## Two New Executives, Two New Mandates

In November 2025, VPG announced the creation of two C-suite positions that had never previously existed in company history. Yair Alcobi was appointed Chief Business and Product Officer, responsible for centralized product strategy and business development across all three segments. Rafi Ouzan was named Chief Operating Officer, charged with standardizing operational execution across a manufacturing footprint spanning Israel, North Carolina, India, Germany, Sweden, Canada, and Rhode Island. Their combined mandates were designed to fill a structural gap that had existed since the spinoff: between segment-level general managers and Shoshani himself, there was no intermediate executive layer capable of coordinating product roadmaps and operational priorities across the company's distinct franchises.

The proxy's biographical descriptions of both executives establish their pre-VPG careers, though their track records within VPG remain unproven as of the snapshot date. What is clear from the organizational logic is that Shoshani is preparing for a growth phase that his prior organizational structure was not built to execute. A CEO managing segment heads directly while simultaneously leading investor relations, evaluating M&A targets, and articulating the robotics thesis to institutional capital cannot also be the de facto product strategist and operational integrator. Alcobi's mandate — product strategy across sensors, weighing, and measurement systems — addresses the need for a coherent portfolio narrative. Ouzan's mandate — operational standardization — addresses the need for execution velocity. Whether their combined capabilities are equal to the demand environment they have been hired into will be visible in VPG's operating margins and bookings conversion over the next four to six quarters.

## A Board Between Generations

VPG's board of seven directors — six independent, one executive — reflects both the company's founding governance commitments and a deliberate refreshment effort over the past four years. Saul Reibstein, 77, has served as non-executive Chairman since the 2010 spinoff; his background as an accounting and audit professional provides the financial oversight foundation that the audit committee requires. Timothy Talbert, 79, chairs the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee and has served since 2010, bringing institutional continuity to board process.

The more recent additions mark a deliberate shift toward technology and capital markets competence. Sejal Shah Gulati, 52, joined in 2022 with a background in technology commercialization and corporate governance. Erez Lorber, 61, joined in 2024 with a financial investment background. Nava Swersky Sofer, 60, also joined in 2024, bringing life sciences venture capital and independent-director experience to the governance mix. Kobi Altman, 57, joined in 2025. The board's age distribution — with Reibstein at 77 and Talbert at 79 alongside four directors between 52 and 61 — will itself become a governance refreshment question at the 2027 and 2028 annual meetings, particularly if the company's strategic agenda accelerates toward robotics and defense-adjacent M&A that may benefit from directors with direct technology commercialization experience.

Director compensation consists of a $50,000 annual cash retainer ($110,000 for Chairman Reibstein), committee chair stipends, and $80,000 in annual RSU grants. The board's five-times annual retainer ownership requirement creates alignment incentive, though recently appointed directors are unlikely to have met it as of the snapshot date.

## The Zandman Bloc and What It Protects — and Concentrates

The most structurally significant governance fact about VPG is not the board's composition but the 35.1% voting bloc held by the Zandman family through Class B convertible super-voting shares and an informal voting agreement among family members. This concentration means that no activist investor, no strategic acquirer, and no proxy advisory firm can force board change without family consent. There is no disclosed private-equity sponsor. The dual-class structure has drawn scrutiny from governance-focused institutional investors as a general matter, but the 2025 operating performance provides a counterpoint to the entrenchment argument: below-target results triggered no payout of performance-based cash bonuses and no vesting of 2023-vintage performance RSUs, a pay-for-performance outcome that operated independently of the family's voting control.

The protections available to ordinary shareholders are structurally conventional: a six-of-seven independent board supermajority, independent audit and compensation committee composition, and separation of the Chairman and CEO roles. Whether ISS or Glass Lewis has formally flagged the dual-class structure in recent proxy seasons is not disclosed in VPG's public filings, though both advisory firms maintain standard adverse policies on super-voting structures absent a clear sunset provision — and VPG's Class B shares carry no disclosed convertible trigger or sunset date.

## The Compounded Risk of a Leadership Inflection

The picture that emerges is of a company navigating what amounts to a leadership transition at exactly the wrong — or exactly the right, depending on one's interpretation — moment in its operational history. A CFO with fifteen years of institutional knowledge is departing during the first bookings acceleration in a generation. Two new C-suite executives are learning their roles in real time as the robotics design-in pipeline matures from prototype orders toward production commitments. A CEO whose irreplaceability is simultaneously VPG's greatest governance asset and its most underacknowledged succession risk has no visible internal heir apparent. And the Zandman family's voting control, while providing strategic continuity, means that the governance levers available to external shareholders to accelerate management change — were one needed — are limited.
